# Abstract

This randomized controlled trial investigated the efficacy of a novel intervention for treating chronic pain in adults. We enrolled 200 participants and randomized them to treatment (n=100) or placebo (n=100) groups.

# Introduction

Chronic pain affects millions of people worldwide and represents a significant healthcare burden. Current treatments have limited efficacy and significant side effects. Novel approaches are needed to address this unmet medical need.

Previous research has shown promising results with similar interventions in animal models. However, translation to human populations has been challenging.

# Methods

## Study Design

We conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial at three academic medical centers between January 2023 and December 2024.

## Participants

Adults aged 18-65 with chronic pain (>3 months duration) were eligible for inclusion. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy, active malignancy, and concurrent use of opioid medications.

## Intervention

Participants received either the active intervention (100mg daily) or matched placebo for 12 weeks.

## Outcomes

The primary outcome was change in pain score on the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) at 12 weeks. Secondary outcomes included quality of life measures and adverse events.

## Statistical Analysis

We used intention-to-treat analysis with mixed-effects models for repeated measures. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

# Results

Of 200 enrolled participants, 185 (92.5%) completed the 12-week follow-up. Baseline characteristics were similar between groups.

The treatment group showed significantly greater reduction in VAS scores compared to placebo (-2.4 vs -0.8 points, p<0.001). Quality of life measures also improved significantly in the treatment group.

Adverse events were mild and similar between groups. The most common side effects were headache (15%) and nausea (8%).

# Discussion

Our findings demonstrate that the novel intervention significantly reduces chronic pain compared to placebo. The effect size observed is clinically meaningful and compares favorably to existing treatments.

Several limitations should be noted. First, the 12-week follow-up period may not capture long-term effects. Second, our population was predominantly from academic medical centers, which may limit generalizability.

These results have important implications for clinical practice. The intervention offers a new treatment option with a favorable safety profile.

# Conclusion

This randomized controlled trial provides strong evidence for the efficacy of the novel intervention in treating chronic pain. Further studies are needed to evaluate long-term outcomes.
